description: This looks like an immaatation of the Fantastic Four, but it is actually an imitation
summary: Our CLPS Lunar Mission Browser makes lunar south-pole mission planning fast and understandable. Pick a landing site and date, and see where the Sun and Earth sit against real terrain, whether a lander would have power and a direct radio link, and how long until sunset or Earthset. Everything is computed from NASA SPICE kernels and LOLA terrain. Sun and Earth positions match a recomputation to under 0.01 arcseconds, and 115 automated tests pass. Beyond the brief, we added DSN station checks, solar energy estimates, landing-safety data, and a Viable / Marginal / Not viable verdict. We also built a Jordanian shuttle that launches from Jordan and flies to the Moon, landing on Mons Mouton Plateau, the site that never loses sight of Earth. One tool for planners, students and everyone in between: NASA's data, made clear enough for anyone to decide using our AI agent that is build for them all
details:
Overview

The CLPS Lunar Mission Browser lets anyone pick a lunar landing site and a date, then see where the Sun and Earth are, whether a solar lander would have power and a radio link, and how long until sunset or Earthset. Every number comes from NASA SPICE ephemeris kernels and LOLA terrain, computed in the browser. It is our NASA Space Apps 2026 entry (team The Fantastic Four), built on the repo taimashard0/projectF.

The site has three pages behind a shared header (Journey · Build Your Launch · Moon Explorer), each with a back arrow:

1. Journey — a space scene (Moon in the foreground, Earth's night side, the Sun on Earth's limb) and a button that flies the camera to Earth.

2. Build Your Launch — the Jordan rocket on the left, two menus on the right (rocket model, launch site) and a Start button that plays a launch animation from the pad to the Moon.

3. Moon Explorer — a QuickMap-style 3D Moon that opens on the full disk and zooms to the south pole, with the site-and-date dashboards beside it and analysis tabs below.

A floating Ask AI mission assistant sits on every page (interface only, not yet connected to a model).

Live version: CLPS Lunar Mission Browser. Local copy: run Open website.bat in the project folder.

The data

All data is real and listed with its source; nothing is invented or demo data. Geometry everywhere uses the MOON_ME frame, planetocentric latitude, east-positive longitude, azimuth clockwise from north, and the 1737.4 km reference sphere.

Dataset

What it holds

Source

How it was checked

Ephemeris (ephem.bin)

Sun and Earth vectors from the Moon's centre every 30 minutes, 2026-01-01 to 2030-12-31 (87,648 samples, 2.1 MB)

NASA NAIF SPICE: naif0012.tls, pck00011.tpc, de440s.bsp, moon_pa_de440_200625.bpc, moon_de440_250416.tf; MOON_ME, LT+S

Recomputed with SpiceyPy from the uploaded kernels: worst difference 0.007″ (Sun), 0.002″ (Earth); 48 golden az/el rows match to 0.00003°

Terrain horizons (horizons/*.json)

Skyline angle every 0.5° of azimuth for the 11 analysed sites, for 2, 10 and 20 m masts

LOLA PGDA LDEM_80S_20MPP_ADJ (to 30 km) and LDEM_60S_240MPP_ADJ (to 200 km), Barker et al. 2023

Pipeline validation checks (Shackleton floor permanently shadowed, rim among best-lit, higher mast never raises the horizon)

Custom-point terrain (dem/)

LOLA 240 m DEM tiles to compute a horizon at any point from ~83° S to the pole

LDEM_60S_240MPP_ADJ

Against the named sites' 20 m horizons: worst-site median 0.51°, 90th percentile 1.44°

Eclipses

Visible share of the Sun disk when Earth passes in front of it, per site

Same SPICE vectors in the browser; eclipses.json lists SPICE gfoclt events

Pipeline check: formula vs gfoclt

DSN mask (dsn.bin)

Per sample, which of Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra see the Moon above 10°

DSN 810-005 station coordinates + SPICE Earth rotation

Pipeline check vs NASA precise station kernels

Polar grid (grid.json + heat maps)

5 km grid of % sunlit, % Earth visible, longest shadow, elevation

Pipeline over LOLA + SPICE

Compared with NASA published illumination and Earth-visibility maps

Artemis III regions (regions.json)

NASA's nine candidate regions and the chosen point in each

USGS/NASA region file (McClernan 2024)

Points inside outlines, slope ≤ 5°, 100 m circle safe

Site catalogue (catalogue.json + catalogue.ts)

Apollo 11–17, IM-1, IM-2, Blue Ghost 1, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Chang'e-4/5/6, Luna 17, planned IM-3 and Draper targets

NASA NAIF CLPS kernels, LROC, NSSDC, NASA CLPS pages; each entry carries its source

Planned targets are labelled as feature centres, not landing points

Imagery and radioactivity

LROC WAC/NAC mosaic tiles, Lunar Prospector thorium

Lunar QuickMap tile service (public domain)

Tile grid alignment verified on the pole; thorium palette decoded from QuickMap's own colour table

The 11 analysed sites are IM-2 Athena, the Shackleton rim high point, and one engine-selected point in each Artemis III region (Haworth, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton, Mons Mouton Plateau, Nobile Rim 1 and 2, de Gerlache Rim 2, Slater Plain, Peak near Cabeus B).

The metrics

Every metric is built from three per-sample series computed for the chosen site and mast: sunlit, Earth in view (DTE) and DSN link. Durations are counted in 30-minute samples and clipped at the edges of the chosen period.

Metric

Definition

Where it appears

Sun / Earth elevation and azimuth

Angle of the body's centre above the flat horizon, and its compass direction, seen from site elevation + mast

At this moment; skyline; comparison

Terrain toward the Sun / Earth

LOLA skyline angle at that body's azimuth for the chosen mast

At this moment (Detailed)

Visible Sun fraction

Share of the Sun disk (radius 0.267°) above the skyline, times the eclipse factor

At this moment

Sunlit

Visible Sun fraction ≥ 0.5 (editable in the timeline tab)

Status chip, % sunlit, sunlight periods

Earth in view (DTE)

Earth-centre elevation minus the skyline at its azimuth ≥ 0° (editable margin)

Status chip, % DTE, visibility windows

Earth clearance

Earth elevation minus the skyline at its azimuth

At this moment

DSN link

DTE and at least one DSN station has the Moon ≥ 10° up

Status chip, % DSN, longest DSN gap

Longest shadow / longest Earth blackout

Longest unbroken run of not-sunlit / not-DTE samples

Mission window; 2026–2030 record; comparison

Time to sunset, sunrise, Earthset, Earthrise

Time from the chosen sample to the next change of the sunlit or DTE series

At this moment; comparison; skyline countdowns

Solar irradiance

1360.8 W/m² × (1 AU / Sun distance)² × visible Sun fraction × cos(Sun elevation), for a vertical array that turns to face the Sun

At this moment; mission window

Solar energy

Irradiance summed over the window × 0.5 h, in kWh/m² (also given for a flat deck panel, using sin of elevation)

Mission window; Power tab; comparison

Thorium

Lunar Prospector gamma-ray thorium averaged around the site (0.5° bins, ~15 km), in ppm

2026–2030 record; Radioactivity layer

Viability of a site and date. A mission window starts at the chosen time and lasts 1, 7, 14 or 29.5 days. Power passes when sunlight ≥ 70% and the longest shadow ≤ 50 h; communication passes when Earth is in view ≥ 80% and the longest blackout ≤ 24 h. Both pass = Viable, one = Marginal, none = Not viable. The defaults come from the team's landing study and every limit is editable in the Power and communication tab.

The trade-off is clear: Shackleton's rim has the most sunlight but loses Earth for up to two weeks, while Mons Mouton Plateau never loses Earth but has long nights.

The website, page by page

Shared header

A pill header (Journey · Build Your Launch · Moon Explorer) marks the current page, plus a back arrow on the top left. Pages have their own links (#journey, #build-your-launch, #moon-explorer), so browser Back/Forward and refresh work, and the launch choice survives navigation.

1. Journey

A calm 3D space scene after the team's reference photo: the Moon in the lower-left foreground, Earth's night side with city lights, and the Sun rising past Earth's limb. "Let's start the journey" and the Begin on Earth button fly the camera to Earth, which opens the next page. Without WebGL a still fallback is shown.

2. Build Your Launch

The team's Jordan rocket (red body, white seven-pointed star, black, white and green boosters) stands on the left against a moving sky with drifting clouds. On the right are two boxes: Rocket model (Jordan rocket, Starship, Falcon 9, SLS, Ariane 6, Electron) and Launch site (eight real launch sites), each with a one-line description, and a Start button. The Jordan rocket is a cut-out of the team's render; picking another rocket swaps in a turning 3D model of it.

3. Launch animation

Ignition and smoke on the pad, liftoff into a sunset sky, the sky fading to black, then space with Earth below and a flight to the Moon. The chosen rocket flies (including a 3D Jordan rocket), a mission clock and phase labels run on the left, and Skip jumps straight to the explorer.

4. Moon Explorer

The map. One textured 3D Moon. It opens on the full disk, then flies straight to the south pole on the same sphere (no page change). Left rail: Full Moon, Layers, Landing sites, Map settings, Date and time, Mission data. Top right: zoom in, zoom out, south-pole overview. Bottom: latitude/longitude/resolution readout and a scale bar. Imagery streams from Lunar QuickMap and sharpens as you zoom; the LOLA relief view is in Map settings. The Moon is lit by the real Sun at the chosen time, and gold and blue arrows at the selected site point to the Sun and Earth (faint when below the horizon).

Layers menu: Sunlight (heat map), Longest shadow, Radioactivity (thorium), Earth visibility, plus Artemis III region outlines and opacity.

Beside the Moon, from the top:

* Plain text: "Site information — Select a landing site on the Moon or in the list to open its dashboard", or the chosen site's name and coordinates; a Simple / Detailed switch.

* Site & date box: grouped site list, Previous/Next site, Custom coordinates, mast height, date and time (UTC), ±1 h and ±1 day steps, Now, Play the lunar day with speed, and mission length.

* At this moment: Sunlit / Earth in view / DSN chips, a one-line verdict, Sun and Earth position against the skyline, solar power, and countdowns to sunset or sunrise and Earthset or Earthrise.

* Mission window: Viable / Marginal / Not viable with the four checks, DSN link, energy and highest Sun.

* 2026–2030 record: the original dashboard — % sunlit, % DTE, % DSN, longest shadow, longest blackout, thorium, pipeline cross-check, landing safety (slope, roughness, distance to permanent shadow), calculation rules and sources.

* Layers box.

Tabs below the map:

Tab

What it shows

Sky and horizon

360° skyline from LOLA with the Sun and Earth paths over one lunar day (click a path to jump to that time), countdowns, and a draggable lunar-day timeline of Sun and Earth height above the skyline with sunlit, Earth and DSN bands

Power and communication

Power and communication cards, every sunlight period and Earth visibility window in the mission, and editable viability limits

Compare sites

Any sites side by side at the same date and mast; best value per row highlighted; Show on Moon / Remove

2026–2030 timeline

The original year/month/day charts and calendar heat map for one site or several, with editable thresholds

How it works

Plain-language guide: how to use it, why the pole is special, a lunar day, why Earth hardly moves, a glossary, data sources

Below the tabs, a Scientific validation table lists every pipeline check with its result and tolerance.

5. Mission assistant (all pages)

A gold Ask AI button bottom-right opens a chat panel: site and UTC date pickers, a one-click "Use the Moon Explorer's site and time", suggested questions, chat bubbles and a typing indicator. When the chat's site and time match the explorer, each question carries the explorer's 16 numbers (shown under "Data sent with the question"). It is the interface only: src/agent/agentApi.ts is the one function to connect to a model, and until then it says clearly that it is not connected. Chat history is kept across pages.

Engineering

The site is static React 19 + TypeScript + Vite + Three.js: no server, all calculations run in the visitor's browser from files in public/data. 115 automated tests pass (Vitest), and the production build is checked in a headless Chrome on desktop and phone sizes.

Folder / file

Role

src/lib/geometry.ts, windows.ts, eclipse.ts

Site frame, Sun/Earth alt-az from the ephemeris, sunlit/DTE/DSN series, range metrics, eclipse factor

src/lib/moment.ts, countdown.ts, power.ts, comms.ts

At-this-moment readout, mission-window viability, sunset/Earthset countdowns, solar irradiance and energy

src/lib/terrainHorizon.ts, gridHorizon.ts

Horizon at any south-pole point from the LOLA 240 m DEM

src/lib/catalogue.ts

Curated sites, groups and custom-point ids

src/context/MissionContext.tsx

Loads all data once; caches tracks and eclipse factors; builds custom points

src/map/LunarScene.tsx, quickmap.ts, CommandMap.tsx

3D Moon, QuickMap tile streaming, layers, real-Sun lighting, arrows, the boxes beside the Moon

src/views/

MomentPanels (boxes), MissionInsights (tabs), SkylineView, LunarDayStrip, TimelineView

src/journey/

Journey, Build Your Launch, launch animation, rocket models (incl. the Jordan rocket), header

src/agent/

Mission assistant UI, the context it shares, and agentApi.ts where a model is connected

pipeline/ (team repo)

Python + SpiceyPy scripts that produce the data files from the kernels

Tests cover SPICE geometry against golden values, horizon engine, eclipse and DSN layers, reproduction of the pipeline numbers for all 11 sites, terrain horizons at custom points, power and comms, countdowns, the QuickMap palette, and physical sanity (Apollo 11 sunlit ~50% with two-week nights and Earth always up; Chang'e-4 never sees Earth).

Hosting. The live artifact serves the binary data as base64 text because that host refuses .bin files, and it cannot load QuickMap tiles, so it shows the built-in LOLA terrain instead. Running locally (Open website.bat) or on any static host gives the live imagery.

Saving the work. The changes are in update.zip; unzip it over the projectF folder on the Desktop, then commit and push from VS Code to Aseel03/projectF.

Limits and next steps

These are the points a judge may ask about; the site states each of them on screen.

* Dates run 2026–2030. The ephemeris file covers only that window, so Apollo and other past sites show 2026–2030 conditions, not their landing days. The kernels (de440s) cover 1849–2150, so a longer file is a pipeline run away, at about 0.4 MB per year.

* Flat horizons away from the pole. Catalogue sites and custom points outside ~83° S have no terrain model, so hills and crater walls are ignored; this matters most for sunlight near crater edges.

* Custom points use 240 m terrain, not the 20 m used for the 11 analysed sites (typical difference under 0.5°).

* Planned CLPS targets are feature centres (IAU coordinates), not the real landing ellipses.

* Solar power is per m² of array with no panel efficiency, temperature or battery model.

* The mission assistant is UI only. Connecting it means implementing askAgent in src/agent/agentApi.ts against a model API, with the explorer's numbers already attached to each question.

* Live imagery was tested with stand-in tiles in the cloud test browser; it needs a check on a real machine with internet.

Next steps, in order of value: connect the assistant; extend the ephemeris to cover Apollo dates and the Artemis era; add terrain for the catalogue sites; and run the launch and explorer pages on the presentation laptop before the event.
